statements.text: Government use of Artificial Intelligence poses significant and potentially positive outcomes but also significant challenges – particularly surrounding ethical use and data security. [...] I think it is the duty of Congress to examine both the positives and negatives of AI prior to authorizing what is likely to be billions of dollars for decades.

statements.text: We can see the dangers of run-away AI use in China. Using AI to support genocide in Xinjiang and suppress democracy in Hong Kong provides insight into how our adversaries view and use this technology – as a way to suppress dissent and to become a global economic and military power.
statements.venue: Opening statement, joint House Oversight subcommittee hearing on the future of AI

statements.text: AI is moving quickly, and while it can increase efficiency and productivity, we can’t ignore the potential risks to students, workers, and privacy. [...] Technology should serve workers, not replace them, and it should support education without undermining academic integrity or fairness.
statements.venue: Grothman e-newsletter on Education & Workforce Committee hearing

statements.text: The rapid pace of AI development is not an excuse for Congress to rush into policy without careful consideration. Our workforce, our students, and our economy deserve thoughtful, practical solutions that protect Americans while allowing innovation to move forward responsibly.
statements.venue: Grothman e-newsletter on Education & Workforce Committee hearing

statements.text: How one looks at religion, it could affect how someone looks at politics, it could affect how someone looks at history. And one of the things that scares me it people get a hold of this, you’ll push a politically correct view on all these topics.

statements.text:
At @EdWorkforceCmte’s “Building an AI-Ready America” hearing, I raised serious questions about how artificial intelligence is being rolled out in classrooms and workplaces.

AI may offer productivity gains and new tools for training, but Congress has a responsibility to ensure it doesn’t undermine workers, weaken academic integrity, or put privacy at risk. As these technologies scale quickly, policymakers need to understand where AI is helping, and where it could create real problems for students and workers.
These tools can be invaluable for augmenting worker safety, but there must be space for human oversight, and employers should be wary of delegating ultimate responsibility for worker safety to AI.
statements.venue: Opening statement, Workforce Protections Subcommittee hearing on AI and workplace safety

statements.text: One of my concerns about A.I. is that it could lead to a decrease in human involvement in the workplace due to over-involvement in technology.
statements.venue: Higher Education and Workforce Development Subcommittee hearing on AI, as quoted by Seehafer News

statements.text:
No one in Wisconsin’s Sixth District should have to pay higher electricity bills to subsidize the infrastructure needed for a data centers.

That’s why I’m supported the Ratepayer Protection Act. As America leads the AI race, we need to ensure these major investments don’t leave families and small businesses footing the bill for the energy infrastructure they require.

We can support innovation while protecting Wisconsin ratepayers.

We recently passed a bill -- the Ratepayer Protection Act -- in Congress, which should make sure that new data centers were covering the charges for water, were covering the charges for electricity, and I think that will be a big step in the right direction

I enjoyed meeting with the Institute of Internal Auditors’ Fox Valley Chapter to discuss data privacy, AI risks, and strengthening internal oversight of artificial intelligence. As AI becomes more widespread, strong oversight, clear standards, and protecting Americans’ personal information are essential to managing emerging risks and ensuring responsible innovation.

We should pass laws preventing people from putting phony images of somebody on the internet. That being said, I'm not for as much regulation as some other people. Regulation benefits the big guy, right? I don't care what business you're in and we want new people in the field at all times.

We don't want artificial intelligence to be something like 1984 where we have just a few people out there and those people are answerable to the government and make sure your view of history or your view of current events is that what is what the the powers to be want.
